Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old woman with 3–4 months of progressive painful, cracked, itchy palmar skin consistent with suspected contact dermatitis related to recent housekeeping work; started emollient and antihistamine without benefit; plan for topical steroid, stronger emollients, trigger avoidance, and follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Soreness, cracking, and intermittent itch of the skin of the hands, primarily affecting the palms; occasional bleeding when scratched.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began approximately 3–4 months ago after a job change to hotel housekeeping.
  - Gradually worsened to the point of significant pain and work impairment; has been unable to work for the past three days.
- Exacerbating/initiating/relieving factors:
  - Likely related to occupational exposure to cleaning products and inconsistent glove use while working as a housekeeper.
  - Avoidance of triggers (glove use) recommended; prior over-the-counter emollient (E45) and an antihistamine were tried and reported as ineffective.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary symptoms.
  - General appetite and well-being reported as maintained.
  - Mild generalized dry skin noted on legs historically.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior diagnosed eczema or other skin disease (patient reports no known prior skin diagnoses).
  - No asthma or bowel disease reported.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (no further details provided; on metformin).
- No other medical conditions reported.
- No prior diagnosis of eczema or dermatitis reported.

Medications:
- Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- OTC emollient E45 (tried, ineffective) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Antihistamine (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) — tried, ineffective.

Allergies:
- No known drug or other allergies.

Social History:
- Occupation: Housekeeper in a hotel; cleans bedrooms, bathrooms, corridors; uses bathroom cleaning products.
- Protective equipment: Reports inconsistent glove use at work.
- Smoking: Denies tobacco use.
- Alcohol: "A couple of pints a week."
- No illicit substance use reported.
- Recent job change ~4 months ago (temporal relation to symptom onset).
- Work impact: Unable to work for past three days due to hand symptoms.

Family History:
- Family history of diabetes.
- No known family history of skin disease reported.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented.
- No physical examination findings documented in the transcript.

Investigations:
- No investigations or test results were ordered or reported.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Suspected contact dermatitis / occupational dermatitis of the hands (palmar predominant)
  - Assessment:
    - Clinical impression by clinician: dermatitis or contact dermatitis related to occupational cleaning exposure and inconsistent glove use.
  - Plan:
    - Advise strict avoidance of triggers: wear protective gloves when cleaning.
    - Initiate topical steroid cream — medication name/dose/route/frequency not documented (prescription to be sent to pharmacy).
    - Start stronger emollients to be applied frequently (patient instructed to coat skin 3–4 times daily) for the next couple of weeks.
    - If no improvement within ~1–2 weeks (10–14 days) or if worsening/spreading occurs, return for review sooner.
    - Prescription to be sent to patient’s pharmacy.
- Issue 2: Type 2 diabetes mellitus — chronic condition
  - Assessment:
    - Patient is on metformin; no acute diabetes issues reported during this visit.
  - Plan:
    - No change to diabetes management documented.
- Issue 3: Work limitation related to hand symptoms
  - Assessment:
    - Symptoms currently preventing work; patient has missed work for three days.
  - Plan:
    - Advise protective measures (gloves) and treatment as above to enable return to work; no formal work note or specific occupational health referral documented.

General Plan items:
- Follow-up arranged if symptoms not improved in 1–2 weeks or earlier if worsening or spreading.
- Prescription to be sent to pharmacy during the consult.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs and focused physical examination of the hands (appearance, extent of cracking, erythema, fissures, secondary infection signs) were not documented.
  - Specific name, dose, route, and frequency of the prescribed topical steroid were not documented.
  - No documentation of whether a sick note or occupational health referral was provided.
  - No allergy verification beyond patient report.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - None identified.
- Transcript quality:
  - Conversation is intelligible and sufficient to extract relevant clinical history and the clinician’s assessment and plan; portions of the physical exam and precise prescription details were not recorded in the transcript.
